body:
Why is a launch vehicle needed?

An artificial satellite cannot enter orbit merely by being lifted above the atmosphere. It must also acquire enough sideways velocity to travel around Earth under gravity.

A launch vehicle is a rocket system that carries a spacecraft or other payload from Earth and gives it the required motion to reach a specified trajectory or orbit. Its purpose is different from that of the satellite: the launch vehicle provides transportation, while the satellite performs its mission after deployment.

A rocket that travels high above Earth but does not acquire the motion needed for a sustained orbit may follow a suborbital trajectory and return towards Earth. Thus, reaching a great height and entering orbit are not the same achievement.

How a launch normally proceeds

Although different launch vehicles follow different flight sequences, the basic process can be understood in 5 stages.

  1. Lift-off: The rocket's engines produce thrust sufficient to raise it from the launch pad.
  2. Ascent and direction change: The vehicle climbs and gradually develops the required sideways motion for its intended orbital path.
  3. Stage separation: When a stage has completed its useful powered flight, it is detached so that later stages do not have to carry its empty mass.
  4. Fairing separation: The protective covering around the payload is discarded when the vehicle has passed through the denser part of the atmosphere and the covering is no longer needed.
  5. Orbit insertion and deployment: The final powered portion of the flight provides the required motion, and the satellite is released into its designated orbit or transfer trajectory.

The exact timing varies by rocket and mission. For example, strap-on boosters may burn alongside a central rocket stage, while the principal stages are separated in sequence.

Stages, boosters, payload and fairing

A stage is a powered section of a rocket used during part of the flight. Multistage launch vehicles discard used stages because reducing unnecessary mass helps the remaining vehicle continue accelerating.

A strap-on booster is an additional rocket motor attached to the main vehicle to provide thrust, particularly during the early part of ascent. A booster is not necessarily a separately numbered principal stage.

The payload is what the rocket carries for the mission. During a satellite launch, the payload normally includes the satellite or satellites and may include associated deployment equipment.

The payload fairing is the protective covering around the payload during ascent through the atmosphere. It protects the spacecraft from aerodynamic forces and other effects of atmospheric flight. The fairing is part of the launcher, not the working satellite's scientific or communication payload.

Launch vehicle: transports the satellite. Satellite: performs the mission. Payload fairing: protects the satellite during launch. Rocket stage: supplies propulsion during part of the journey.

Direct injection and transfer-orbit launch

Some satellites are launched directly into or near their intended low Earth orbit. Others, particularly satellites intended for GEO, may first be placed in an elliptical transfer orbit.

For a geostationary mission, the launch vehicle may inject the satellite into GTO. Once separated, the satellite's onboard propulsion system performs additional manoeuvres to reach its final orbit. This explains why a successful GTO injection does not mean the satellite has already reached GEO.

India's launch location

India's principal spaceport is the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. It provides launch-base infrastructure, launch operations and associated tracking facilities for Indian space missions.

For suitable eastward launches, Earth's rotation can contribute to the rocket's initial eastward motion. The intended orbit and safe flight path also influence the direction of launch. A rocket designed for a polar mission follows a different trajectory from one intended to support an equatorial or geostationary mission.

Prelims focus

  • Entering orbit requires suitable sideways velocity, not merely a high altitude.
  • Multistage rockets discard completed stages to reduce unnecessary mass.
  • Strap-on boosters provide additional thrust and may operate alongside the main stage.
  • The payload fairing protects the spacecraft during atmospheric ascent.
  • SDSC SHAR at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is India's principal launch centre.
  • Trap: Insertion into GTO is not the same as arrival in the final GEO.

[Sources: European Space Agency, 'Types of orbits', introductory discussion and 'Transfer orbits and Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO)' section, published 30 March 2020; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark II', sections 'Payload Fairing' and 'CUS (Third Stage)'; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'PSLV', sections 'Payload Fairing' and 'Vehicle Specifications'; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) SHAR', centre overview; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: From Launch Pad to Orbit: What a Rocket Does

body:
How does a rocket produce thrust?

A rocket engine expels gases or other propellant products backwards at high speed. The rocket experiences a force in the opposite direction and moves forwards. This is an application of Newton's third law of motion: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

A chemical rocket generally carries both a fuel, which releases energy, and an oxidizer, which supports the chemical reaction. It does not depend on taking oxygen from the surrounding air. This is why rockets can operate above the atmosphere and in the vacuum of space.

Solid and liquid propulsion

Rocket propulsion is commonly classified according to the physical form and storage of its propellants.

Solid-propellant rocket motors

In a solid rocket motor, the fuel and oxidizing components are incorporated into a solid propellant. Once ignited, the material burns and produces high-pressure gases that leave through a nozzle, generating thrust.

Solid motors are comparatively straightforward to store and use. They can provide substantial thrust and are commonly employed during launch and in boosters. A conventional solid rocket motor, however, generally cannot be shut down and restarted as readily as a controllable liquid engine.

Liquid-propellant rocket engines

In a liquid rocket engine, fuel and oxidizer are stored as liquids and supplied to the engine, where they react and produce thrust. Depending on the engine design, liquid propulsion can provide greater control over starting, stopping or adjusting thrust.

Liquid engines are used in several stages of Indian launch vehicles. The Vikas engine is a well-known example of a liquid-propellant rocket engine used in Indian launch vehicles.

Cryogenic propulsion

Cryogenic propulsion uses propellants stored at extremely low temperatures. Indian cryogenic rocket engines use liquid hydrogen as fuel and liquid oxygen as oxidizer.

Liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen can provide high propulsion efficiency. However, storing and using them requires special arrangements because the liquids must be maintained at very low temperatures.

Cryogenic propulsion is a type of liquid propulsion. The distinction concerns the very low temperatures needed to store its propellants. It is not a third physical state of matter separate from solids and liquids.

How Indian launch vehicles combine propulsion systems

India's launch vehicles demonstrate how different propulsion systems can be combined according to the payload and intended orbit.

Launch vehicleBasic configurationPrincipal role
PSLV4 main stages: solid, liquid, solid, liquid.Especially associated with polar and Sun-synchronous satellite launches; also used for other mission types.
GSLV Mk II3 stages: solid core with liquid strap-ons; liquid second stage; cryogenic upper stage.Launching satellites towards geosynchronous transfer orbits.
LVM33 main propulsion stages: 2 solid strap-on boosters, liquid core stage and cryogenic upper stage.Heavy-lift missions to GTO and LEO.
SSLV3 solid propulsion stages plus a liquid-propulsion Velocity Trimming Module.Launching small satellites, particularly into low Earth orbits.

PSLV: Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle

The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is closely associated with India's Earth-observation missions. Its 4 principal stages alternate between solid and liquid propulsion:

  1. First stage: solid propulsion.
  2. Second stage: liquid propulsion.
  3. Third stage: solid propulsion.
  4. Fourth stage: liquid propulsion.

PSLV is particularly useful for placing satellites in low polar and Sun-synchronous orbits. The name Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle does not mean that PSLV can launch only polar-orbiting spacecraft. It has also served other types of missions.

GSLV Mk II: Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle

The GSLV Mk II is a 3-stage launcher. Its first stage includes a solid central motor assisted by 4 liquid strap-on motors. The second stage uses liquid propulsion, while the third stage uses a cryogenic engine.

The cryogenic upper stage is particularly important for placing the satellite on the high-energy transfer path needed for a geosynchronous mission. The rocket may release the satellite in GTO, after which the satellite performs its own orbit-raising manoeuvres.

LVM3: a heavier-lift launch vehicle

Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3), also associated with the earlier name GSLV Mk III, is a heavier-lift launcher.

Its principal propulsion arrangement comprises 2 solid strap-on boosters, a liquid-propellant core stage and a cryogenic upper stage. LVM3 is designed to place comparatively heavy payloads in Earth orbit or transfer orbits.

The presence of 2 solid boosters does not make LVM3 a 2-stage vehicle. It is described as a 3-stage launch vehicle based on its principal propulsion sequence.

SSLV: Small Satellite Launch Vehicle

The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) is intended for comparatively small satellites. It has 3 solid propulsion stages and a separate liquid-propulsion Velocity Trimming Module (VTM) for final velocity adjustments.

Its published design capability includes launching a satellite of approximately 500 kg into a 500 km orbit, under specified mission conditions. These are design-performance figures, not the mass or altitude of every SSLV mission.

Remember the propulsion patterns: PSLV alternates solid and liquid stages; GSLV Mk II uses a cryogenic third stage; LVM3 combines 2 solid boosters, a liquid core and a cryogenic upper stage; SSLV combines 3 solid stages with liquid velocity trimming.

Expendable and reusable launch systems

Many traditional rockets discard stages that are not recovered for another flight. Such systems are described as expendable. A reusable launch system is designed to recover and use at least some of its hardware again.

Reusability is a characteristic of how a launch system is used after flight. It does not itself identify whether the rocket uses solid, liquid or cryogenic propulsion, nor does it specify the orbit of its payload.

Prelims focus

  • Rockets produce thrust by expelling material backwards and can operate in vacuum without atmospheric oxygen.
  • Solid rocket motors generally cannot be stopped and restarted as readily as many liquid engines.
  • Cryogenic Indian rocket engines use liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
  • PSLV has 4 main stages in the order solid–liquid–solid–liquid.
  • GSLV Mk II and LVM3 use cryogenic upper stages; SSLV uses 3 solid stages plus liquid velocity trimming.
  • Trap: A cryogenic engine uses liquid propellants, and the number of boosters is not necessarily the number of main stages.

[Sources: Indian Space Research Organisation, 'PSLV', sections 'Vehicle Specifications' and 'First Stage' through 'Fourth Stage'; 'Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark II', sections 'GS1', 'GS2' and 'CUS'; 'LVM3 (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mk III)', sections 'Vehicle Specifications' and 'About the Launch Vehicle'; 'Small Satellite Launch Vehicle', sections 'Vehicle Configuration', 'Velocity Trimming Module' and 'About the Launch Vehicle'; all consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'GSLV-D5/GSAT-14: Indigenous Cryogenic Stage', cryogenic propulsion description; consulted 4 November 2026.]
